bodyHtml:
The core course teaches you to read the chart through liquidity, structure and imbalance: where the stops are, where price displaced, where it may come back to. This track has taught you to read volume and order flow: where business was done, and how. This chapter puts the two side by side. They were developed by different communities and use different words, but at key prices they often describe the same thing from two angles.

The aim is not to add more lines to your chart. It is to use one method to check the other. When a liquidity level and a profile level agree, you have a clearer reason to care about that price. When they disagree, you have learned something too.

Where is the liquidity?

SMC / liquidity tool (core course): Equal highs and lows, old swing points (ch 07).

Profile / order-flow tool (this track): Poor highs and lows, naked POCs (VP-02, VP-05).

Where did price move fast?

SMC / liquidity tool (core course): Fair value gaps (ch 10).

Profile / order-flow tool (this track): LVNs and single prints (VP-02, VP-03).

Where did it do business?

SMC / liquidity tool (core course): Order blocks: the last opposite candle before displacement (ch 09).

Profile / order-flow tool (this track): HVNs, POC and value area (VP-03).

Cheap or expensive?

SMC / liquidity tool (core course): Premium and discount of a range (ch 11).

Profile / order-flow tool (this track): Above or below value; VWAP and bands (VP-01, VP-06).

Was the sweep real?

SMC / liquidity tool (core course): Wick through, close back, sharp reversal (ch 12).

Profile / order-flow tool (this track): Absorption or trapped traders on the footprint (VP-09).

Fair value gaps, LVNs and single prints

A fair value gap is a three-candle pattern: the wick of candle 1 and the wick of candle 3 don't overlap, and the gap between them is the FVG (chapter 10). A low-volume node is a price range where little volume traded (VP-03). Single prints are TPO rows with only one letter (VP-02). All three are measures of the same event: price moving quickly through a range without two-sided trade.

Here the FVG runs from 5,201.75 to 5,205.25, and the thinnest part of the profile sits in the same place. That overlap is common but not guaranteed. An FVG is measured on one timeframe's candles, while the profile counts every contract, so a gap on a 5-minute chart can contain a surprising amount of volume if it formed across a busy minute. When the FVG and the LVN coincide, both methods are telling you price has not traded there much. When they don't, the profile is the more direct measurement of how much trade actually happened.

The core course says price often returns to FVGs, and gives the common explanation that orders were left unfilled there. Profile traders describe LVNs in a similar but more cautious way: the market moved through them without accepting them, so on a return it tends either to move through quickly again or to reject them. Neither description means price must come back.

Order blocks, HVNs and the POC

In the core course an order block is the last opposite-colour candle before a displacement: for a bullish order block, the last down candle before the move up (chapter 09). Profile traders would ask a different question about the same place: how much volume traded there? If the order block sits on a high-volume node or a POC, the market did real business at that price before it left. If it sits in thin volume, the "block" was a brief pause. That is a useful filter when you have several candidate order blocks and need to choose one.

Premium, discount and value

Premium and discount split a swing range at its 50%% midpoint (chapter 11). The value area is where 70%% of the volume traded. They measure different things. Premium and discount are geometry: halves of a price range. Value is measured participation. On a P-shaped day, for example, most of the value sits in the upper, "premium" half of the range. Profile traders would read buying there as buying at value, not buying expensive. When the two methods disagree like this, it is worth asking which question you are really trying to answer.

Liquidity sweeps, LVNs and the footprint

A liquidity sweep in the core course has three parts: price trades through a known level, closes back on the original side, and reverses with conviction (chapter 12). The profile and the footprint each add a check.

Profile check. The wick reached into a low-volume node from an earlier profile. Price moving quickly into an LVN and being rejected is the auction version of "no acceptance". If the wick had instead reached a high-volume node and started building volume there, that would suggest the market was accepting the lower prices, which argues against a sweep.

Footprint check. Here is the sweep bar, row by row:

PriceBid x ask
5,229.7514 x 11
5,229.5038 x 22
5,229.2561 x 35
5,229.0088 x 40
5,228.7572 x 38
5,228.5054 x 33
5,228.2547 x 30
5,228.0041 x 29
5,227.7533 x 24
5,227.5029 x 26
5,227.2522 x 31
5,227.0019 x 35
5,226.7516 x 38
5,226.5012 x 34
5,226.259 x 21

The bar's total delta is -108: sellers were the aggressors overall, and 442 contracts were sold at the bid below the lows. That is the stop-loss selling and breakout selling the sweep was expected to trigger. But look at the bottom five rows: at every one of them, more traded at the ask than at the bid. Aggressive buyers appeared at the lows of the wick, and price closed back above the level. The sellers who sold the break are now trapped (VP-09).

Put together: a liquidity level (equal lows), a profile level (the LVN), and a footprint pattern (selling absorbed, buyers at the lows, trapped sellers) all pointing the same way. That is what "confluence" means in practice: independent methods agreeing, not the same method drawn twice.

When the two methods disagree

Disagreement is not a problem to be explained away. It is information. Three situations come up often.

  • A sweep into a high-volume node. Price runs the lows, but the wick lands in a busy area of the profile and starts building more volume. The market is doing business at the lower prices, which is acceptance. Many profile traders would expect the move to continue rather than reverse.
  • An FVG with plenty of volume inside it. The candle chart shows a gap, but the profile shows real two-sided trade there. The "imbalance" was a matter of how the candles happened to be drawn, and the level deserves less weight.
  • An order block in thin volume. The last opposite candle before the move was brief and light. Little business was done, so there is less reason to expect anyone to defend it.

In each case the profile is a direct measurement of trade, while the candle pattern is a shape. When they conflict, give the measurement more weight, and write down which one turned out right. After a few months your own journal will tell you how the two methods behave on the instrument you trade, which is worth more than any general rule.

Worked example: a combined pre-session plan

  1. Bias (core course). The higher timeframe is bullish: structure is making higher highs and higher lows.
  2. Value (VP-05). Value has migrated higher for three sessions. Yesterday's VAL sits just above a set of equal lows.
  3. Liquidity (ch 07). Those equal lows hold sell-side liquidity.
  4. Thin area (VP-03). Below the equal lows there is an LVN left by a fast move earlier in the week, overlapping an unfilled bullish FVG.
  5. Scenario. If price sweeps the equal lows into the LVN and the footprint shows selling absorbed and buyers at the low, the long scenario from your playbook applies. If instead price builds volume inside the LVN and holds below the lows, value is moving lower, and the bullish scenario is off.

Notice that both outcomes are written down before the session. The combination doesn't tell you which will happen. It tells you what each one would look like, so you can recognise it when it does. Position size and the stop still come from your risk plan (chapter 36), and this is a hypothetical example, not a recommendation.

Common mistakes

  • Counting the same idea twice. An FVG and an LVN from the same leg are one event measured two ways, not two reasons.
  • Forcing agreement. If the profile disagrees with your liquidity read, take that seriously instead of hunting for another tool.
  • Using spot or CFD data for the profile. Build the profile on the future (VP-10).
  • Treating premium as always "expensive". Value can sit in the premium half of a range.
  • Drawing everything. Five well-chosen levels beat twenty.

Key takeaways

  • FVGs, LVNs and single prints all describe fast one-sided movement, measured three ways.
  • Volume at an order block tells you whether real business was done there.
  • Premium/discount is geometry; value is measured participation. They can disagree.
  • A sweep into an LVN with absorption on the footprint is the strongest form of the combined read.
  • Write both scenarios down before the session.

Practice exercises

  1. For ten recent FVGs on a 5-minute ES chart, anchor a fixed-range profile to the leg. How many sit on an LVN?
  2. Take your last five order-block entries. Was each one on an HVN, an LVN, or neither?
  3. Find three liquidity sweeps. Check the profile level the wick reached and the footprint of the sweep bar.
  4. Write a combined plan like the worked example for tomorrow's session, then review it at the close.

Self-check quiz

1. What do an FVG, an LVN and single prints have in common?

They all mark price moving quickly through a range without two-sided trade.

2. How can volume help you choose between two order blocks?

Prefer the one where more business was done, such as one on an HVN or POC.

3. Why can value sit in the premium half of a range?

Premium/discount is geometry; value follows where volume actually traded, as on a P-shaped day.

4. What footprint evidence supports a sweep of equal lows?

Selling at the bid below the lows that fails to hold, with buyers appearing at the wick low and a close back above.

5. Why isn't an FVG plus an LVN from the same leg two separate reasons?

Because both measure the same fast move; they are one event seen two ways.

Sources

  2. Fixed Range Volume Profile indicator - TradingView Help Center
  3. Time price opportunity charts explained - TradingView Help Center
  4. Volume Footprint charts: a complete guide - TradingView Help Center
  5. Order Flow Volumetric Bars - NinjaTrader 8 Help Guide
  6. Mind Over Markets, Updated Edition (Dalton, Jones, Dalton; Wiley 2013) - further reading
